A-en.profile: Grassroots, founded 2023, 4 staff (2 full time), about $310K budget. A neighborhood-rooted violence interruption and youth mentoring group in its third year. Credibility with young people and families is its greatest asset; nearly all back-office function runs through the founder and executive director. Funding is one city contract plus small individual gifts.

conversation: If our founder or executive director were out for a month, which tasks would stop, and who could pick them up?

How many months could we pay everyone if the city contract paid late or ended?
What does success look like for a young person in our program, and how would we know?
Who outside our team, such as a parent, a young person or a partner, should help shape our first written plan?

steps: Hold one team meeting to write 3 to 5 goals in plain words for the next 12 months.
Make a simple table with goals, activities, a timeline and an owner for each. Do this for outreach and for mentoring.
Draw a simple logic model: what you do, then what you hope changes for young people and the neighborhood. The BJA checklist (Step 3.1) explains how.
Keep it to two pages. Post it where staff can see it.
focus.title: Write a one-page work plan the whole team shares
focus.why: You told us you do not yet have written work plans, a logic model, or a strategy. Much of your direction lives in your founder's and executive director's heads. A short written plan lets your team and funders see what you do and why. Planning also tends to lift Fundraising and Financial Management, so it unlocks the most.

steps: List what money you expect each month for the next 12 months and the date it should arrive, starting with the city contract payment schedule.
List what you must pay each month, with payroll first.
Mark any months where money out comes before money in, and decide what you would do in those months.
Ask the city contractor how quickly invoices are paid, and set a monthly 30-minute cash check.
focus.title: Make a short cash plan so payroll is safe
focus.why: Meeting payroll steadily is the base of staff trust. Your money comes mostly from one city contract plus small gifts, so a late payment could hit pay fast. A simple look ahead at cash lets you spot timing gaps early and calmly.

report.summary:
Southside Youth Peace Collective is a young group with deep roots. You started in 2023. You now run street outreach and youth mentoring with a team of 4 and a budget near $310K. Young people and families trust you. That trust is hard to build, and it is your biggest asset.

All four areas we looked at (Planning, Fundraising, Financial Management, and Monitoring, Learning and Evaluation) are at the Seeding stage. Seeding means the basic building blocks are just being laid. That fits an organization in its third year. Much of the back-office work runs through your founder and executive director. That works for now, but it puts a lot on two shoulders.

You already have good pieces in place. You use an accounting system. You share financial duties. You have an annual budget. You track who you serve. You know where funding will come from for the next 6 to 12 months. The next step is to write things down and share the load. We suggest two places to start. They are a simple written work plan and a steady payroll cushion. Together they protect your people and make later funding and data work easier.

B-en.profile: Mid-size, founded 2016, 19 staff, about $2.1M budget. An established CVI provider operating hospital-based intervention and street outreach across two precincts. Core systems exist and are used, but they are uneven: the board is functioning yet thin on finance expertise, and evaluation is still mostly output counting. Roughly 80% of revenue is restricted government funding.

conversation: If our largest government grant ended in six months, which hospital and outreach roles would be at risk, and what would we do first?
Which funders could we ask for multi-year or flexible support this year, and who will make the ask?
What do our staff find hardest about collecting data, and what one change would make it easier?
What do we want to be able to say about changes in safety or participant lives, beyond how many people we served?
What finance skills would help our board most, and where could we find that help?

steps: List every funder, the amount, what it can be spent on, and the end or renewal date.
Mark each line as confirmed or pending, and add up each month's expected income.
Compare the map to your program commitments in the hospital and on the street, and note any months with a gap.
Share the one-page map with your board and leadership team and update it monthly.
focus.title: Map your next 12 months of funding
focus.why: Most of your revenue is restricted government money, so it matters a lot to know what is confirmed, what is pending and when each grant ends. Your answers show you plan ahead in many ways. This one item shows you can still get a clearer, shared view of the next year. A clear map helps you decide what you can promise your hospital and street outreach teams. It also tells you when to start asking funders for more.

steps: Write a one-page guide that says what to record, when, and in which tool, for both the hospital team and the outreach team.
Hold a short hands-on training, such as a lunch-and-learn, for all staff who enter data.
Add a quick data check to regular one-on-one supervision so the habit sticks.
Ask staff what is hard about the tools and fix the biggest pain point first.
focus.title: Train every staff member to use data the same way
focus.why: Your team already uses standard tools and reviews data together. But not everyone has been trained to collect and use data in the same way. Your data is mostly counts right now. Steady, trusted data is the base for showing funders what changes because of your work. It also makes it easier to move past counting later.

plan.owner: Executive director, with the bookkeeper or finance lead
steps: Put every funder, amount, use limits and end date on one sheet.
Label each line confirmed or pending, and show income month by month.
Mark any months where hospital or outreach staff costs are not yet covered.
Review the sheet with leadership and set a monthly update day.
plan.title: Build the 12-month funding map
plan.why: With most revenue restricted and from government, a clear view of confirmed and pending money lets you make safe choices about staffing and programs.

steps: Write a one-page guide for data entry: what to record, when and where, with plain definitions.
Run a short training for hospital and outreach staff using real examples.
Pick one person to answer data questions in the first month.
plan.title: Write a simple data guide and run a first training
plan.why: Staff need the same rules for collecting data before you can trust it or build on it.

steps: Check each program commitment against confirmed funding and flag any at risk.

plan.why: Knowing when money ends helps you avoid over-promising, and a longer view helps you plan before grants run out.

steps: Add a five-minute data check to each one-on-one supervision.

plan.why: Training only sticks when it is reinforced. A named data lead also gives you steady quality and a base to grow evaluation.

steps: Ask a finance-savvy volunteer, advisor or new board member to review your budget work.
Draft a two-year budget that includes the full cost of supervision, data, training and transportation.
Confirm who owns each tax and filing deadline and write the dates on a shared calendar.
plan.title: Build a multi-year budget with board finance help
plan.why: Your board works well but is thin on finance expertise. Planning beyond one year needs strong finance voices at the table.

steps: Choose two or three outcome measures for each of hospital and street outreach, such as how often participants stay engaged. Ask community members what success looks like.
Collect them for 90 days using your standard tools.
Use the results, along with consent-based participant stories, in your next proposal.
plan.title: Add a few outcome measures and use them in funding asks
plan.why: Your data mostly counts activity. A few measures of change give funders a stronger story at the $25,000 to $75,000 level and above.

steps: Assign a named person, or a part-time consultant, to lead fundraising tasks.
List five funders that give $75,000 or more and match them to your priorities.
Plan a first relationship step for each, such as an intro call or a site visit.
Look at how peer grantees tell their stories and borrow what fits.
plan.title: Give fundraising a clear owner and a funder relationship plan
plan.why: Larger and multi-year grants come from relationships built before the application. Someone needs time set aside for that.

report.summary:
Here's what I've learned about you. Riverbend has been doing this work since 2016. You run hospital-based intervention and street outreach across two precincts, with a team of 19. You are an established group with real systems that your team uses. Your Planning and Financial Management are at the Developing stage. Your Fundraising and your Monitoring, Learning and Evaluation are at the Emerging stage. This is a learning tool, not a grade. It shows where you are today and where to build next.

You are strong in planning and money basics. You keep written work plans for the next 6 to 12 months and check your progress against them. You review financial reports with leadership and the board, you track spending by program and funding stream, you hold reserves, and you do an independent audit every year. You also have a written fundraising plan, and you have funding that lasts beyond one year. On the data side, your programs have defined outcomes, your team uses standard tools, and you review data together and share it with funders and partners. Those are real foundations.

You are a little weaker in a few connected places. Most of your money is restricted government funding, so it is hard to see clearly what is confirmed and what is still pending. Your data work is mostly counting what you do, and not every staff member is trained to collect and use data the same way. Your board works well but could use more finance know-how. If I were you, I would start with two things. First, build a clear 12-month picture of your funding, with confirmed money in one column and pending money in another. Second, train your staff to collect and use data the same way every time. These two steps are small and doable. They also make every later funding conversation stronger.
